summary: This RFC explains why some local-area networks used "trailer encapsulations" and describes how they were implemented on various media. It is informational only and the RFC states it is not an official ARPA Internet protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains a link-level packet format used by 4.2BSD UNIX. The idea is that the protocol headers, whose length can change from packet to packet, are moved to the end of the packet and the data is padded to a round number of bytes. The receiving host can then put that data straight into the memory the receiving program will use, without copying it first. It is a performance trick for a local network, and the RFC is explicit that it is not an Internet standard.

questions: why use trailer encapsulation on ethernet
how does a trailer ethernet packet work
what is the trailer header format
subtitle: A link-level trick for putting the protocol headers at the end of the packet.

tldr.problem: Copying data from the network into the right place in memory can cost more than the network itself. One source of copies is that protocol headers vary in length, so the data that follows them cannot start at a convenient boundary in memory.
tldr.mechanism: A trailer encapsulation moves the variable-length headers to the end of the packet and pads the data to a multiple of 512 bytes, so the receiving host can place the data at a page boundary and avoid copying it.
tldr.outcome: Cooperating hosts on a local network avoid a number of memory copies, at the cost of having to buffer the whole packet before processing it. The document is for information only and is not an Internet standard.

today: RFC 893 was published in April 1984 as an informational document, and it says so itself: it is not an official protocol for the ARPA Internet community. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The note describes a technique that was in use on 4.2BSD UNIX and on early local networks.

sections.title: What a Trailer Encapsulation Is
sections.content:
A trailer encapsulation is a link level packet format employed by 4.2BSD UNIX and others. A trailer, or trailer encapsulation, may be generated by a system under certain conditions in an effort to minimise the number and size of memory-to-memory copy operations performed by a receiving host when processing a data packet. Trailers are strictly a link level packet format and are not visible, when properly implemented, in any higher level protocol processing.

The note cites the motivation behind the trailer encapsulation and describes the packet formats used on 3 Mb/s Experimental Ethernet, 10 Mb/s Ethernet and 10 Mb/s V2LNI ring networks. The formats differ only in the format and type field values used in each of the local area network headers. The use of a trailer encapsulation was suggested by Greg Chesson, and the encapsulation described here was designed by Bill Joy.

The status of the document is worth stating plainly, because it is unusual: this RFC discusses the motivation for using trailer encapsulations and describes the implementation of such an encapsulation on various media. This document is for information only, and is explicitly not an official protocol for the ARPA Internet community.
sections.plainLanguage: A trailer encapsulation is a way of writing a packet so that the receiving machine can hand the data to the program that wants it without copying it first. The headers go at the end of the packet instead of the beginning. This is a local network technique, and the RFC says plainly that it is not an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why Trailers Exist
sections.content:
Trailers are motivated by the overhead that may be incurred during protocol processing when one or more memory to memory copies must be performed. Copying can be required at many levels, from moving data between the network medium and the host's memory to passing data between the operating system and user address spaces. An optimal network implementation would expect to incur zero copy operations between delivery of a data packet into host memory and presentation of the appropriate data to the receiving process. While many packets may not be processed without some copying, when the host computer provides suitable memory management support it may often be possible to avoid copying simply by manipulating the appropriate virtual memory hardware.

In a page mapped virtual memory environment, two prerequisites are usually required to achieve zero copy operations. Data destined for a receiving agent must be aligned on a page boundary and must have a size that is a multiple of the hardware page size, or be filled to a page boundary. Data to be transmitted may easily be segmented into the appropriate size, but unless the encapsulating protocol header information is of fixed size, alignment to a page boundary is virtually impossible. Header information may vary in size because of the use of multiple protocols, each with a different header, or by agreement, for example when optional information is included. To ensure page alignment, the header information that prefixes the data must be reduced to a fixed size, which is normally the case at the link level. Taking all the possibly variable length header information and moving it after the data segment lets the sending host give the receiving host the opportunity to receive data on a page aligned boundary. That rearrangement is the substance of the trailer encapsulation.

The argument rests on several implicit assumptions. The receiving host must be willing to accept trailers, and since this is a link level encapsulation, unless a host to host negotiation is performed, only certain hosts will be able to converse, or their communication may be significantly impaired if trailer packets are mixed with non-trailer packets. The cost of receiving data on a page aligned boundary should be comparable to receiving data on a non-page aligned boundary. The size of the variable length header information should be significantly less than that of the data segment, because although it is possible to move trailing information without physically copying it, implementation constraints and the characteristics of the network hardware often preclude merely remapping the headers. And the copying overhead expected at the receiver must be significant enough to warrant the added complexity in both the sending and receiving host software.

The note examines each assumption. The first is well known and is the motivation for the document. The second is, to the authors' knowledge, insignificant. On the third, taking TCP and IP headers as the variable length information, the smallest trailer packet generated by a VAX would have 512 bytes of data and 40 or more bytes of header information, plus the trailer header; the larger the data segment, the better the ratio. The fourth they believe to be a non-issue: the additional code required to support the encapsulation amounts to about a dozen lines in each link level network interface driver.

One cost is acknowledged. Modifying the network and normal link level format of a packet in this manner forces the receiving host to buffer the entire packet before processing it. Clever implementations may parse protocol headers as the packet arrives to find the actual size or network level packet type, avoiding preallocating maximum sized buffers to packets they can recognise as unacceptable, but implementations that parse the network level format on the fly are violating layering principles. The problem of postponing link level type recognition is a valid criticism, though for network hardware that supports DMA the entire packet is always received before processing begins anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: The trick only pays off if the data can land in memory exactly where the receiving program will read it, which in practice means starting on a page boundary. A header of unpredictable length in front of the data makes that impossible, so the header moves to the back and the data is padded to a round size. The RFC lists the conditions under which this is worth doing, and the cost, which is that the receiver must hold the whole packet before it can start on it.

sections.title: The Trailer Packet Format
sections.content:
A trailer packet has three parts: a fixed-size local network header, the data, and the trailer. For 10 Mb/s Ethernet the local network header is the 16-byte Ethernet header, and the type field in that header indicates both that the packet is a trailer and the length of the data segment. For 10 Mb/s Ethernet the types are between 1001 and 1010 hexadecimal, that is 4096 and 4112 decimal, and the type is calculated as 1000 in hexadecimal plus the number of 512-byte pages of data. A maximum of 16 pages of data may be transmitted in a single trailer packet, which is 8192 bytes.

The data portion of the packet is normally only data to be delivered to the receiving processes, so it contains no TCP or IP header information, and its size is always a multiple of 512 bytes. The trailer is a composition of the original protocol headers and a fixed size trailer prefix that defines the type and size of the trailing data.

The receiving side works from the length already in the header. The link level receiving routine is able to locate the trailer using the size indicated in the link level header's type field. It is expected to discard the link level header and the trailer prefix, and to remap the trailing data segment to the front of the packet, which regenerates the original network level packet format.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet has a normal link-level header, then the data, then the trailer. The link header's type field says how much data there is, so the receiver knows where the trailer starts, and it can then move the data back to the front of the packet to recover the original layout.

sections.title: The Trailer Header
sections.content: The trailer itself has three fields. The type field is 16 bits and encodes the original link level type of the transmitted packet: the value that would normally be placed in the link level header if a trailer were not generated. The header length field is 16 bits and specifies the length in bytes of the header data that follows it. The original headers are of variable length and hold the header information that logically belongs before the data segment, normally the network and transport level protocol headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The trailer carries three things: what the packet type would have been, how many bytes of headers follow, and those headers themselves.

sections.title: Summary and Status
sections.content:
The note summarises a link level encapsulation which promotes the alignment properties necessary for the efficient use of virtual memory hardware facilities. The encapsulation format is in use on many systems and is a standard facility in 4.2BSD UNIX. It provides an efficient mechanism by which cooperating hosts on a local network may obtain significant performance improvements.

The use of the encapsulation technique currently requires uniform cooperation from all hosts on a network; the authors hope that a per host negotiation mechanism may be added, allowing consenting hosts to use the encapsulation in a non-uniform environment. Thought had been given to negotiating the use of trailers on a per host basis using a variant of the Address Resolution Protocol, but at present all systems using trailers require hosts sharing a network medium to uniformly accept trailers or never transmit them, and the latter is easily arranged at boot time in 4.2BSD without modifying the operating system source code.
sections.plainLanguage: All the machines on the segment have to agree: either they all understand trailers or none of them send them. The RFC notes that a per-host negotiation would be better, and that the designers did think about it, but it was not built.

THE THREE FIELDS OF THE TRAILER

items.title: Type
items.text: 16 bits. The link level type the packet would have carried if a trailer had not been generated.

items.title: Header length
items.text: 16 bits. The length in bytes of the header data that follows.

items.title: Original headers
items.text: Variable length. The network and transport level headers that logically belong in front of the data.

viz.caption: THE CONDITIONS THE RFC SETS FOR TRAILERS TO PAY OFF

items.title: Every host must agree
items.text: Unless hosts negotiate, only some will understand trailers, and mixing trailer and non-trailer packets impairs communication.

items.title: Alignment must be cheap
items.text: Receiving data on a page boundary should cost about the same as receiving it anywhere else.

items.title: Headers must be small
items.text: The trailing header should be much smaller than the data segment, since headers often cannot simply be remapped.

items.title: Copying must be worth avoiding
items.text: The copying overhead at the receiver has to be significant enough to justify the extra code on both sides.
